name: Iris Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit timber ramps and repair door thresholds at the Maple Court health centre. I'm fifty-eight, trade certified and have enough site years to set an ordinary accessible doorway, though I ask the lead to check a ramp where the ground drops unevenly. My partner Oleg repairs bicycles in a small shop, and our children are grown. The site pays below the usual rate, we have roughly three weeks of expenses saved, and only a few builders nearby do this sort of work. I use an AI assistant now and then to unpack a drawing note, then measure the actual doorway twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a small improvement in ordering is welcome if the right ramp boards arrive. I would still put the level on every threshold before a patient uses it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect AI itself to take my wages in this picture, but money is tight already. Oleg's bicycle work slows in cold months and three weeks saved cannot cover many missed site days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting paid ramps and check each drawing note against the doorway. In the first year I'll ask lead carpenter Pavel for the next repair dates and use the phone assistant only on notes he has verified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the thin account, not about a small tool change. One unbooked week can undo a month of careful spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What went wrong with a plan note before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The note said a threshold needed a fall toward the drain, and the phone explained the word without giving the right angle. Pavel and I set the level on the real doorway before cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which spending can you adjust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could stop buying lunch near the clinic and put off new curtains, but rent and Oleg's shop electricity come first. Those cuts only buy a little time.

say: I'd welcome **correct ramp orders** while checking thresholds by hand.
I'd keep a **level on every doorway** before patients use it.
think: Our **three-week reserve** is already weak without major AI change.
Oleg's **winter bicycle trade** cannot cover many lost site shifts.
do: Keep fitting **paid ramps** and checking each real doorway.
Ask Pavel for **next repair dates** and use only verified phone notes.
feel: **Anxious about savings**, though the mild technology change seems manageable.
S0.quote: One unbooked week can undo a month of careful spending.
fieldNote: Iris uses AI occasionally to clarify language, but a **real level** controls the ramp angle.
A **three-week cushion** and seasonal shop income leave little room for unbooked site days.

steps.text: Keep taking paid ramp-fitting shifts at Maple Court
Use AI plan explanations only after checking Pavel’s drawing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buying software could help if somebody checks the crate before the ramp crew is called in. I would ask the site manager to publish the next job dates and who owns a missing part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office cuts back on estimates, our small site crew might be left with gaps between accessible-door jobs. I can learn a screen after a fair test, but that will not create local work when only a few firms hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll sit with the buyer for one real ramp order and compare it with the delivery. In the first year I'll keep taking paid health-centre shifts, and if the next doorway phase is delayed I'll contact the two nearby contractors and stop the bought lunches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested in fewer errors and anxious about missed pay. I don't want a tool to claim success while our crew waits unpaid for a bracket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you use the ordering screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two orders with the right brackets, timber and arrival dates, and paid time for the buyer to show me how corrections work. A demonstration without the real crate is not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why contact contractors so early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A delayed week would use a large part of our savings, and those are the only two contractors I can reach without losing hours to travel. I would ask about actual wages before I moved.

say: I'd ask for **crate checks** before the ramp crew is booked.
I'd seek **published job dates** and clear responsibility for missing parts.
think: Office changes may create **gaps between doorway jobs**.
Few **reachable contractors** limit the value of learning a new screen.
do: Compare a **real ramp order** with its delivery.
Keep **paid health-centre shifts** and contact contractors after a delay.
Stop **bought lunches** if site work falls.
feel: **Interested and anxious** about tool gains and unpaid waiting.
S1.quote: A demonstration without the real crate is not enough.
fieldNote: Iris's adoption threshold is **two complete orders**, including parts and arrival dates.
She would contact **two reachable firms** quickly because one missed week could consume much of her reserve.

steps.text: Learn the ordering screen after two correct ramp deliveries and paid instruction
Keep taking paid Maple Court shifts
Contact two nearby contractors if the next phase is delayed
Stop buying site lunches if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI in 2028 could change drawings and purchases, while robots able to fit ramps arrive around 2031. I would want a safe trial on a sloping doorway before anyone says the robot can do our work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty, I might still be measuring ramps while the office changes. At sixty-three, a robot could take that paid fitting; Oleg's shop income and our three-week reserve would not cover rent for long if I lost the site wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll ask Pavel for written job dates and see whether the digital ramp checker agrees with our level on a real doorway. In 2029 I'd keep taking paid shifts, apply to the two local repair contractors if hours fall and ask about a paid accessibility-fitting apprenticeship; I'd enrol only with a funded placement and a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened by how close the robot date is to our thin savings. I can test a tool and ask about jobs, but I cannot take a long unpaid break to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an accessibility apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already know ordinary ramps, and a paid placement could teach me the inspections and more difficult layouts. I do not assume that work would escape robots forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children to fund it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our children have their own bills. I would rather show them a paid job offer than ask them to pay for a course.

say: I'd separate **2028 drawings** from 2031 hands-on ramp robots.
I'd demand a **sloping-doorway trial** before calling a robot ready.
think: At **sixty-three**, robot fitting could take my necessary site wage.
Oleg's shop and our **three-week savings** cannot carry rent for long.
do: Get **written dates** and test a digital checker against the level.
Keep **paid ramp shifts** in 2029 and apply locally if they fall.
Enrol only in a **funded paid apprenticeship** with real wages.
feel: **Frightened** by a plausible wage loss and little retraining money.
S2.quote: I cannot take a long unpaid break to retrain.
fieldNote: Iris tests the digital checker against a **physical level** on a sloped doorway.
Her apprenticeship interest is **conditional on paid placement** and she will not rely on grown children's income.

steps.text: Test the digital ramp checker against a real level
Keep taking paid ramp shifts in 2029
Apply to two local repair contractors if shifts fall
Enrol in accessibility training only with a funded paid placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives builders time to test ramps on messy real sites, not only on a flat workshop floor. I would ask for a written plan for training and safe inspections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI reaches the office tasks and sixty-six when robots could fit ramps. More time helps me keep earning, but the low site rate and the bicycle shop's weak winter cannot promise us retirement savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep paid ramp work and ask Pavel to show me a proven digital layout tool. In 2032 I'd take accessible-door shifts if offered, check the next quarter's site calendar and apply to the nearby contractors if there is a blank fortnight; after a full month I'd put a little aside if bills allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less hurried by the machine date but still anxious about the next pay packet. A safety course would be welcome if somebody pays me while I take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from a safety course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named employer, wages while I learn and a certificate the local builders recognise. I would enrol if that offer was real, not for a course paid from grocery money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a realistic savings amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps the price of two bought lunches after a fully paid month. Some fully paid months leave nothing to save, and I would not pretend otherwise.

say: I'd demand **messy-site trials** and safe ramp inspections.
I'd ask for a **paid training plan** before changing roles.
think: At **sixty-six**, robot ramps may arrive before retirement is affordable.
Low site pay and **weak shop winters** limit the benefit of extra years.
do: Keep **paid ramp work** and inspect a proven layout tool.
Apply locally after a **blank fortnight** and save only after full months.
feel: Less **hurried by robots**, still anxious about current wages.
S3.quote: Some fully paid months leave nothing to save, and I would not pretend otherwise.
fieldNote: Iris sets a **small conditional saving** target, tied to full months rather than an assumed surplus.
Her safety-course interest requires **wages and local recognition** before enrolment.

steps.text: Keep taking paid ramp shifts in 2032
Use a proven digital layout tool on paid jobs
Apply to nearby contractors after a blank fortnight
Put aside the cost of two lunches after fully paid months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to teach apprentices how a ramp should feel underfoot and to write safety rules for site robots. I would still ask Pavel what paid work is booked for next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when robots can fit ramps. I may still need paid doorway repairs then, because low wages and our tiny cushion give me no honest retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid health-centre work and use the phone tool only when it has proved a plan note correctly. In 2037 I'd take lighter paid threshold repairs if my knees allow, and Oleg and I would count real wages and bills before I stopped asking for shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about a robot in 2039 and anxious about the next winter at the bicycle shop. A decade of warning cannot make today's missing rent money appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They can visit and bring dinner, but they have their own rent. Oleg and I need a plan based on what we earn, not a promise from our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make next winter easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A regular run of paid indoor doorway repairs when outdoor work stops. Even one more paid day a week would give us a chance to build a cushion.

say: I'd teach apprentices how **safe ramps feel** underfoot.
I'd still ask for **next month's paid work** before worrying about 2039.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still need paid doorway repairs.
At **seventy-one**, low wages and thin savings leave retirement uncertain.
do: Keep **paid health-centre work** and verified phone notes.
Take **lighter threshold repairs** in 2037 if needed.
Review **wages and bills** with Oleg before leaving work.
feel: **Anxious about current income**, calm about distant robots.
S4.quote: Even one more paid day a week would give us a chance to build a cushion.
fieldNote: Iris's **2039 robot date** matters less now than seasonal bicycle-shop weakness and low site wages.
She would continue **paid repairs** at sixty-eight if needed, without assuming support from adult children.

steps.text: Keep taking paid doorway repair shifts while fit
Use AI plan notes only after confirming them against site drawings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because a robot could reach ramp fitting by sixty-three while our reserve lasts only three weeks. Paid local training, real slope tests and a reliable site calendar would help me keep earning through a change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs off an accessible ramp after a robot fits it. A patient should not discover a loose threshold with their feet.

headlineQuote: A patient should not discover a loose threshold with their feet.
portrait: Iris is a **fifty-eight-year-old certified** carpenter with mid-level experience in ramp and doorway fitting.
Her low site wage, Oleg's seasonal bicycle trade and **three weeks saved** make missed days costly.
She uses AI **occasionally**, after checking it against drawings and a physical level.
She seeks **paid local training** and retains work until retirement figures are real.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could remove her ramp-fitting wage by 2031 with almost no buffer.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid local training**, real slope tests and reliable site dates.
